rdth-01-c1.claim: His essay reached English readers in 1960 in Death and the Right Hand, translated by Rodney and Claudia Needham.

rdth-01-c2.text: Caitlin Zaloom (2020). Mary Douglas, Purity and Danger (1966). New York University, College of Arts and Science (essay PDF).
rdth-01-c2.quote: Although classification systems separate elements and relate them to each other, the same systems also produce anomalies: things, people, or actions that do not fit into the categories. These are dirt, and they invoke fears of pollution.
rdth-01-c2.claim: In Purity and Danger (1966) the anthropologist Mary Douglas argued that dirt is "matter out of place," so what a society treats as polluting reveals how it classifies the world.

rdth-01-c3.text: Chris Fowler, Inigo Olalde, Vicki Cummings, et al (2022). A high-resolution picture of kinship practices in an Early Neolithic tomb. Nature (accepted version, White Rose Research Online, University of York).
rdth-01-c3.quote: reconstruction of a five-generation family including 27 individuals which we co-analyse with contextual archaeological information
rdth-01-c3.claim: A 2021 study of the Hazleton North long cairn in Gloucestershire, England, built around 3700 BCE, identified 27 close relatives spanning five generations.

rdth-02-c1.quote: After death, a dog is brought to view the corpse.
rdth-02-c1.claim: A dog is brought to look at the corpse, the sagdid or "dog's gaze," believed to drive back the Nasu.

rdth-04-c1.quote: The Sa'dan Toraja, a people numbering about 325,000, live in Tana Toraja, the mountainous northern part of the southwest peninsula of the Indonesian island of Sulawesi (formerly Celebes).
rdth-04-c1.claim: The Toraja live in the mountains of South Sulawesi, Indonesia, in the regencies of Tana Toraja and North Toraja.

rdth-05-c1.quote: Within the Merina and Betsileo communities, the reburial of the famadihana (turning over the dead) is a highly celebrated ritual.
rdth-05-c1.claim: Famadihana, literally "turning" and usually rendered "the turning of the bones," is practiced mainly by the Merina and Betsileo of Madagascar's central highlands.
